Philanthropist Chuck Feeney and his wife joined campus leaders for an Oct. 1 ribbon-cutting ceremony at Mission Hall, the new home of UCSF Global Health Sciences and clinical faculty offices. From left to right: Haile Debas, Chuck Feeney, Helga Feeney, Sam Hawgood, Mark Laret and Jaime Sepulveda.
floor vent for cooling air
First floor hallway connects the north and south ends of the building, and offers casual seating for eating or work.
“Town center” spot designed for faculty, staff and students share lunch, read or relax
Full length windows to maximize lighting efficiency.

The first floor is designed so that occupants can see through to all sides of the building from various points along the hallway and lobby. In addition to classrooms, study spaces, and casual tables and chairs, there will be access to laundry facilities, an ATM, and the offices of the audiovisual support team.
The many tall windows of Mission Hall gleam in the morning sun, and the newly planted trees offer some shade in the courtyard.

Philanthropist Chuck Feeney and his wife joined campus leaders for an Oct. 1 ribbon-cutting ceremony at Mission Hall, the new home of UCSF Global Health Sciences and clinical faculty offices. From left to right: Haile Debas, Chuck Feeney, Helga Feeney, Sam Hawgood, Mark Laret and Jaime Sepulveda.

The lower floors of the building contain various sized classrooms, each equipped with state of the art audiovisual equipment. Classes are already in session, though the building’s official ribbon cutting happens Oct. 1.
This study and meeting room offers multiple seating arrangements for a group meeting or solitary work. The left wall is a glass whiteboard where participants can sketch out ideas.
A conference room overlooks the sunlit front lobby. Two-story high windows let light flood the lobby, which overlooks a green space with outdoor seating and will eventually house a café.
Rows of “focus rooms” line the internal walls surrounding each department. The walls block any office sounds, and phone calls taken at one’s desk can easily be forwarded to these private rooms.

The department “neighborhoods” contain desks housed between low-rise walls to allow maximum natural light from the wall of windows. When additional quiet is needed, researchers can retreat to nearby “focus rooms.”

University of California President Janet Napolitano speaks with Sarah Krevans, daughter of Julius Krevans, before the memorial.

Steven Moss, a student pursuing a PhD in chemical biology, holds a large stack of postcards signed by UCSF faculty, staff, students and community members during the "Stand Up For Science" event, to be delivered to House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi.
The UCSF delegation meets with the staff of House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi.
Keith Yamamoto, PhD, vice chancellor for Science Policy and Strategy, speaks in the office of Rep. Peter King of New York, who founded the House NIH Caucus.
A group from the UCSF delegation walks up the stairs to a meeting with Rep. Peter King of New York, who founded the House NIH Caucus.

UCSF postdoc Ivory Dean, PhD, spoke about the need to support diversity in science: “We don’t know where the next cure for disease will come from, but we need to recognize there’s an inherent benefit to include different historically disenfranchised groups, because that kid might be the one that cures cancer.”

More than 40 faculty, postdocs and students participated in a UCSF Advocacy Day in Washington D.C. on April 24, asking their congressional representatives to protect science research funding, health care access and other pressing issues.
UCSF students Jhia Jackson (left) and Allison Wong hold a sign in support of federal funding for research during Stand Up for Science rally.
Stand Up For Science event attendees sign postcards to their congressional representatives, urging them to support scientific research and funding.

Regis Kelly, PhD, director of the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences, or QB3, speaks at the Stand Up For Science Rally outside of Genentech Hall. The rally was organized jointly by UCSF, the California Life Sciences Association and Gladstone Institutes.
Thomas Packard, a postdoc at Gladstone Institutes, attends the Stand Up For Science Rally at UCSF’s Mission Bay campus.
Attendees of the Stand Up For Science Rally on the UCSF Mission Bay campus hold signs advocating for public support of science research.

From left: Deepak Srivastava director of the Gladstone Institute of Cardiovascular Disease; venture capitalist and philanthropist Brook Byers; Hana El-Samad, UCSF associate professor; Sara Radcliffe, president and CEO of the California Life Sciences Association; Paul Hastings, CEO of Oncomed; UCSF Chancellor Sam Hawgood; Cynthia Kenyon, vice president of aging research at Calico; Regis Kelly, director of QB3; and R. Sanders Williams, president of Gladstone Institutes.
A packed Byers Auditorium listens to the UCSF Stand Up For Science Teach-In.
Cherrie Boyer, PhD.

The Stand Up For Science event on Saturday, April 22, started with a UCSF teach-in featuring eight faculty sharing their experiences of pursuing scientific research that has clashed with political sentiments.

A vintage print advertisement for Premarin (conjugated estrogens). In a warmly lit workshop, an older white woman with gray hair, dressed in a light-colored suit, laughs and smiles while standing beside two older men who are examining a wooden object. Hanging lamps and rustic items fill the background, including a large wagon wheel in the foreground. The ad text reads, “help keep her this way,” suggesting happiness and vitality. Below, smaller text describes Premarin as a hormone therapy for menopause.

Vintage black-and-white pharmaceutical advertisement showing a close-up of a woman’s face fragmented by jagged cracks, with small quotes describing menopausal symptoms such as fatigue, hot flashes, and emotional distress. Text on the right reads, “She pays less with Amnestrogen,” promoting conjugated estrogen tablets, with detailed explanatory copy below.

Vintage black-and-white pharmaceutical advertisement depicting an elderly, witch-like figure stirring a cauldron, evoking superstition. Headline reads “Begone Jinniyeh!” with text contrasting old beliefs about menopause with modern estrogen therapy. The ad promotes Di-Ovocylin, an estrogenic drug by Ciba Pharmaceutical Products.

A black-and-white vintage ad for Menrium showing a smiling older couple. The headline reads, “Menrium treats the menopausal symptoms that bother him most.” Dense medical text and dosage information appear on the right, with Roche Laboratories branding at the bottom.

Black-and-white vintage pharmaceutical advertisement showing a woman in a skirt suit holding a handbag, her image split horizontally as if torn in half. Red text reads, “Are you treating only half her menopausal symptoms?” The ad promotes Milprem, a combination of estrogen and meprobamate, with copy describing treatment of both emotional and physical menopausal distress.
